title: Drug Ads Are Deceptive and Deadly
author: Brandon Novick
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/05/Screenshot-2026-05-17-at-6.13.37-PM-680x508.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/05/18/drug-
ads-are-deceptive-and-deadly/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/05/Screenshot-2026-05-17-at-6.13.37-PM-680x508.png)

Photo by [Mikael
Seegen](https://unsplash.com/@mikael_seegen?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText)

Imagine you are sick with a serious medical condition. How would you feel if
someone constantly told you to buy their product because it would cure you,
but this ‘cure’ is actually worse than other treatments and the price tag is
enormous?

This is the [reality](https://www.iqvia.com/locations/united-
states/blogs/2025/10/life-science-and-direct-to-consumer-television-
advertising) of prescription drug advertising. Whether it be on television or
online, drug companies spend billions to tell Americans to buy their products.
In 2024, giant pharmaceutical companies spent over $6 billion on television
alone, and nearly $50 billion in the decade prior.

Yet, these advertisements don’t actually
[include](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11606-017-4274-9#Sec8)
relevant medical facts to prove that a drug is effective. And even more, they
fail to provide evidence of risks. Even the long list of side effects that
narrators are legally required to read off at the end of TV commercials
[often](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2839061) fails to
include all health risks from each drug. Online advertising is worse, as it
frequently fails to mention risks altogether.
[Instead](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/tv-drug-ads-too-emotional-study-
shows/), companies play hopeful music and show healthy, active people playing
sports or otherwise enjoying their lives.

This is because drug advertisements are tools of emotional manipulation.
Companies’ goals are not to share beneficial products with the public; they
want to make consumers think their products will work. If they actually work,
that is a bonus.

[S](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2801060)[tudies](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2800405)
[show](https://www.bmj.com/content/357/bmj.j1855)
[that](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2801060) drug
companies spend more on less beneficial, more profitable treatments and less
on more effective drugs. This coincides with Americans
[spending](https://www.doi.org/10.7249/RRA788-3) three times as much on
prescription drugs in 2022 compared to other wealthy nations. For example,
Americans [spent](https://www.healthsystemtracker.org/chart-collection/how-do-
prescription-drug-costs-in-the-united-states-compare-to-other-
countries/#Per%20capita%20spending%20on%20prescribed%20medicines%20in%20dollars,%20by%20financing%20scheme,%202019%20or%20latest%20year)
423 percent more for the antiinflammatory drug Humira compared to the United
Kingdom, and Ozempic costs nearly $1,000 a month in the US
[compared](https://www.sanders.senate.gov/press-releases/news-sanders-
statement-on-outrageous-cost-of-ozempic/) to $155 in Canada and $59 in
Germany.

These advertisements aren’t just wasteful, they are dangerous. In 2002, Merck
[aired](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xPZQe2IPObs)a television ad for their
antiinflammatory drug Vioxx, showing Olympic gold medalist Dorothy Hamill
figure skating while explaining how Vioxx allowed her to overcome
osteoarthritis pain.

What the advertisement didn’t say was that the company
[knew](https://thehill.com/opinion/healthcare/5178436-pharmaceutical-
transparency-data-rfk/) Vioxx was no more effective than another treatment,
naproxen. Vioxx also increased the risk of heart attacks and strokes. While
Merck raked in billions, the Food & Drug Administration’s Dr. David Graham
[estimated](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736%2805%2917864-7)
[the](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CHRG-112hhrg72917/pdf/CHRG-112hhrg72917.pdf)
drug killed 30,000 to 60,000 Americans.

Merck is by no means the only drug company that has deceived Americans about
its products. From 1991 to 2021, drug companies
[paid](https://www.citizen.org/news/persistent-misconduct-forces-
pharmaceutical-manufacturers-to-pay-62-3-billion-in-penalties/) federal and
state governments more than $22 billion for unlawful promotion of their drugs.
Yet, these fines pale in comparison to the $1.9 trillion the 35 largest drug
companies made between 2000-2018.

Other countries recognize the danger of direct-to-consumer (DTC) prescription
drug advertising, as the United States and New Zealand are the
[only](https://schaeffer.usc.edu/research/should-the-government-restrict-
direct-to-consumer-prescription-drug-advertising-six-takeaways-from-research-
on-the-effects-of-prescription-drug-advertising/) two countries that allow it.
Congress can try to join the rest of the world, as would happen if the
government enacts Senators Bernie Sanders’s and Angus King’s
[ban](https://www.help.senate.gov/dem/newsroom/press/news-sanders-king-
introduce-bill-to-ban-prescription-drug-ads).

Yet, courts will likely prevent the US from banning drug ads because doing so
would violate the free speech protections enshrined in the First Amendment to
the Constitution. Under
[current](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMp078080) legal standards,
ban supporters must show that drug ads are misleading, harmful to public
health, and cannot be sufficiently improved by less restrictive government
policy.

Indeed, drug advertisements do not educate Americans on the true risks and
benefits of medication. They are companies’
[sales](https://www.health.harvard.edu/medications-and-treatments/do-not-get-
sold-on-drug-advertising) pitches meant to get patients to buy their products
even if a different drug or no drug would better serve Americans’ health.
These ads have wasted money on
[less](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2800405)
[effective](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2801060), more
[expensive](https://www.csrxp.org/second-opinion-big-pharmas-advertising-
carries-a-big-price-tag-for-american-patients-and-taxpayers/)drugs while
directly [harming](https://www.citizen.org/article/comments-on-direct-to-
consumer-advertising-of-prescription-drugs/) and killing Americans.

However, courts – especially the [corporate](https://www.levernews.com/the-
supreme-court-is-a-
corporate/)–[friendly](https://harvardlawreview.org/print/vol-135/the-supreme-
court-and-the-pro-business-paradox/) Supreme Court – would likely rule that a
direct ban is not the least restrictive means of stopping harmful drug
advertising.

The Court may be right, as Congress can _de facto_ ban deceitful drug
advertising both on television and online without passing a direct ban.
Congress can and should require companies to clearly mention – visibly and
audibly – all risks from a drug [rather](https://www.hhs.gov/press-room/hhs-
fda-drug-ad-transparency-fact-sheet.html) than today’s weak standards that
came from 1997 federal regulations that
[helped](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3278148/) surge spending on
drug advertising. Violations of this requirement must result in significant
fines that threaten the profitability of the product.

Congress can also eliminate the liability
[shield](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1468-0009.70071?saml_referrer)
protecting drug companies. Americans currently cannot sue drug companies for
misleading and harming them as long as the companies warn doctors or other
drug prescribers of risks.

By forcing companies to spend much of their paid advertising time mentioning
all risks and opening them up to lawsuits, Congress can indirectly ban
deceitful, harmful ads by making them unprofitable. Making drug companies
liable for failing to warn consumers of all risks also better incentivizes
companies to market drugs that are more safe and effective for the American
people.
